children: , the global innovative-medicines company, confronted sharper questions over its dealmaking strategy Friday after clinical setbacks weakened confidence in recent acquisitions. Its U.S.-listed shares traded at $137.58, yet remained roughly 14% lower across five sessions. The picture shows the stock trading 5.36% above its $130.58 GF Value, suggesting the market still prices in a modest premium despite the pipeline turbulence.

CEO Vas Narasimhan has deployed more than $30 billion into acquisitions and partnerships during the past three years, according to Reuters. Now that spending spree faces a harder examination. Artisan Partners has demanded stronger board oversight of acquisitions after del-desiran's failure undermined a central argument for the $12 billion purchase of Avidity. Novartis insists its guidance remains intact and says other medicines acquired through the transaction still have meaningful potential.

The balance sheet reveals why investors are watching closely. Novartis produced $8.9 billion in first-half free cash flow, while acquisitions and intangible-asset transactions consumed $15.3 billionroughly 1.7 times that cash generation. Add $9.1 billion of dividends and $3.1 billion of treasury-share outflows, and the cited cash demands reach $27.5 billion. Net debt consequently surged from $21.9 billion to $39.4 billion, leaving less room for expensive mistakes and raising the pressure on management to turn purchased science into commercial wins.

title: Novartis's $30 Billion Deal Spree Triggers a Boardroom Reckoning
